transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hello, thank you for seeing me. My mind keeps getting stuck on the same worrying thoughts about what I might have forgotten or done wrong, and I can’t seem to shut them off even when I’m not at school. It's just exhausting and I don't know how to make it stop.

Do these thoughts feel intrusive and unwanted, and do you find yourself checking, repeating, or doing any mental rituals to relieve the anxiety? Or are they mainly worries about real-life school stress without any rituals?

Yes, they are definitely intrusive and constantly loop in my head with "what-ifs" about forgetting my dad's pills or messing up school permission slips. To ease the anxiety, I find myself repeatedly rereading emails, rewriting lesson plans, and checking my parents' calendars and pill boxes. I also have to mentally review my plans multiple times before I feel safe leaving school.
Do you recognize that these thoughts and checking rituals are excessive or unreasonable, even though you feel driven to do them? Or do they mostly feel like ordinary worries that make sense to you?

I’m not really sure or haven't thought about whether they are reasonable, to be honest. I just know that in the moment, doing these checks feels absolutely necessary to prevent something bad from happening. If I don't do them, the anxiety that something terrible will happen and it'll be my fault is just too much.
Which bothers you more overall: the unwanted thoughts themselves, or the checking/reviewing rituals you do to feel safe? If one clearly takes up more time or distress, which one is it?

They both bother me deeply but in different ways. The looping "what if" thoughts about my dad's pills or school slips cause the intense mental distress that I just can't shut off, but the actual checking and rewriting rituals are what physically consume my time and keep me from leaving work.

If you had to choose, which is more central to your problem: the intrusive thoughts themselves, or the checking/reviewing rituals you do to reduce the anxiety? Which one takes up more of your day most consistently?

They are closely linked because the looping "what if" thoughts are constantly in my head, but the checking and reviewing rituals are what take up the most actual time. Doing things like rewriting lesson plans, checking pill boxes, and mentally reviewing my work over and over is what consistently keeps me late at school. Those rituals are what take over my day and eat up my evenings.

When you try to resist the checking, rewriting, or mental reviewing, do you usually end up doing them anyway to reduce anxiety, or are the unwanted thoughts present even without doing rituals? Which feels more like the main problem right now?

Trying to resist them is incredibly hard because the "what if" thoughts just keep looping, building up so much anxiety that I eventually feel forced to do the checking and rewriting to prevent something bad from happening. Honestly, both the constant worrying thoughts and the hours I spend doing these rituals feel like a massive, exhausting problem right now.

Even though both are a big problem, if you could magically remove just one, which would help you more: the intrusive “what if” thoughts, or the checking/rewriting/mental reviewing rituals? Which one feels like the true core of the problem?

I think removing the intrusive "what if" thoughts would help the most, because they feel like the true core of the problem. The checking and reviewing rituals only happen because my mind gets stuck on those terrifying loops about my dad's pills or school plans. If I could magically stop those worrying thoughts from starting, I wouldn't feel the overwhelming urge to do the rituals in the first place.

On a typical day, do the intrusive “what if” thoughts take up clearly more time and distress than the checking/reviewing rituals, or are they about equal? If you had to pick one that dominates most days, which is it?

I'm not quite sure which one dominates because they feel so closely linked. The worrying 'what if' thoughts seem to trigger the checking rituals almost immediately, making it really hard to separate which one actually takes up more of my time.

If you estimate the total time in a typical day, do you spend more time stuck in the intrusive “what if” thoughts, or more time doing checking, rewriting, and mental reviewing rituals? Please choose the one that takes more total time most days, even if it’s a close call.

It is really hard to compare because both the thoughts and the rituals feel so constant and overwhelming throughout my day. I'm honestly not quite sure which one takes up more total time because they just blend together.

When the intrusive “what if” thoughts start, are there times you can let them be there without doing any checking, rewriting, or mental reviewing for a long stretch, or do you almost always end up doing a ritual? Which feels more unavoidable on most days: the thoughts themselves or the rituals?

I almost always end up doing the rituals because the anxiety from the "what if" thoughts is just too intense to ignore. I feel like if I don't check or rewrite things, something terrible will happen—like my dad missing a pill—and it will be my fault. Because of that overwhelming fear and guilt, the urge to perform those rituals feels completely unavoidable on most days.

Before the checking or mental reviewing starts, do the unwanted “what if” thoughts ever continue on their own for a long time, or do they usually stop only after you complete the rituals? Which one feels more persistent even after you’ve done the rituals: the thoughts or the rituals?

The "what if" thoughts definitely loop endlessly on their own and don't stop easily, even when I'm just trying to watch a show or fall asleep. Even after I finish checking my parents' pill boxes or rewriting my plans, the anxious thoughts usually persist or return very quickly, which makes me feel like I have to do the rituals all over again.

When these symptoms are at their worst, what takes up more of your total time and distress: the intrusive “what if” thoughts themselves, or the checking/rewriting/mental reviewing rituals? Even if it’s close, please choose the one that is more dominant overall.

It is just so difficult to choose between the two because they feel completely intertwined and equally exhausting. They constantly feed into each other, so I'm really not sure which one is truly more dominant or takes up more of my time overall.

If you were prevented from doing any checking, rewriting, or mental reviewing for a whole day, would the intrusive “what if” thoughts still be a major problem on their own? Or would the rituals be the main thing you feel unable to control?

The "what if" thoughts would definitely still be a massive problem, and they would likely feel even worse because they are what drive my need to check in the first place. Without being able to do the rituals, those looping thoughts and the fear that something terrible will happen and be my fault would completely take over. It would make it absolutely impossible to relax or focus on anything else.

On a typical day, if you add up the time, do you spend more time trapped in the intrusive “what if” thoughts or more time actually doing the checking, rewriting, and mental reviewing rituals? Please pick the one that takes more total time most days, even if it’s a close call.
I honestly haven't timed them to compare, so I'm not quite sure which one takes up more total time. They both feel like they consume so much of my day that it's really hard to separate them.
Even if it’s a close call, which causes more distress overall: the intrusive “what if” thoughts, or the checking/rewriting/mental reviewing rituals? Please choose just one.

While they are closely linked and both are highly distressing, the intrusive "what if" thoughts definitely cause me the most distress overall. They loop constantly in my head, even when I'm trying to relax or fall asleep, and they are what drive me to perform those exhausting checking and rewriting rituals in the first place.

Even though the thoughts cause more distress, if you had to choose which is the main problem overall, would you say it is mostly the unwanted intrusive thoughts, or mostly the checking/reviewing rituals? Please pick the one that feels more central to your OCD.

I would say the unwanted intrusive thoughts are definitely the main, most central problem for me. The checking and rewriting rituals are exhausting, but they only happen because my mind gets stuck on those looping "what ifs" about making mistakes or forgetting things. Those thoughts are what trigger the overwhelming urge to do the rituals in the first place.

Even though the intrusive thoughts feel most central, do you also spend a substantial amount of time every day on the checking, rewriting, or mental reviewing rituals themselves? Or are the rituals relatively minor compared with the thoughts?

The rituals are definitely not minor; I spend hours every day carrying them out. I have to arrive early and stay late at school to rewrite my plans, and I've even left family dinners early just to go back and double-check things. It is incredibly exhausting and consumes a huge portion of my day.
